accepted.title: Use a skill auditor as its own test subject
accepted.summary: An experimental loop tests another skill to evaluate and improve the auditor itself.
accepted.author: @.salt555
accepted.quote: but if i run the skill-audit on the skill-audit skill itself then it just picks a random skill to improve
accepted.explanation: The contributor describes running a custom audit skill against itself. It chooses another skill as a test case, executes that skill in a sandbox, and uses the outcome to revise both the tested skill and the auditor. They schedule the experiment with cron.
accepted.limitations: A community experiment, not a demonstrated guarantee of improvement. The source does not supply a complete implementation. Review proposed skill edits before using them; this is distinct from the built-in security audit command.

review.reason: The distinctive step is recursive evaluation of the auditor using a different skill as its test case. Documentation describes security scans, normal skill testing and automatic skill updates, but not that feedback experiment.

closestDocs.excerpt: hermes skills audit                               # Re-scan all hub skills for security
closestDocs.distinction: This scans installed skills for security; it does not evaluate an auditor by running it against itself.

closestDocs.excerpt: Start a new session and try your skill:
closestDocs.distinction: Normal skill testing is documented. The recursive auditor/test-subject relationship is the community discovery.

accepted.title: Generate the memory vault from a database instead of letting the agent edit it
accepted.summary: Use structured model output as input to a deterministic store, then render a read-only Obsidian view.
accepted.author: @lauratom
accepted.quote: I just have my DB auto-generate a read-only Markdown vault
accepted.explanation: The contributor uses the model to extract structured semantic signals. A Python backend turns those signals into typed nodes and edges in SQLite FTS5, handles memory changes in SQL, and generates Markdown for viewing in Obsidian. The generated vault is an output, not the writable source of truth.
accepted.limitations: Requires a custom memory backend; no complete implementation is supplied in the message. Read-only generated files alone do not establish a security boundary. Built-in Hermes session search already uses SQLite; that alone is not the trick.

review.reason: The unusual inversion is a database-owned memory graph generating a read-only Obsidian view. SQLite session search and memory provider extensibility are documented, but not this specific separation of model output, SQL mutation and a generated vault.

closestDocs.excerpt: All CLI and messaging sessions are stored in SQLite (`~/.hermes/state.db`) with FTS5 full-text search
closestDocs.distinction: Built-in transcript storage is not a structured memory graph that generates an Obsidian vault.

closestDocs.excerpt: Memory provider plugins give Hermes Agent persistent, cross-session knowledge beyond the built-in MEMORY.md and USER.md.
closestDocs.distinction: Documents an extension interface, not the database-to-read-only-vault design.

accepted.title: Let Hermes choose document sections before retrieving pages
accepted.summary: A community demo uses a document hierarchy and targeted tools instead of nearest-vector chunks.
accepted.author: @lemoussel
accepted.quote: The agent first understands how the document is organized, then decides which pages to inspect before answering.
accepted.explanation: The contributor indexes a PDF with PageIndex, waits for indexing, then gives Hermes a toolset dedicated to that document. The agent inspects the hierarchy and chooses relevant pages before answering. This records the retrieval technique, not a recommendation or popularity claim for the project.
accepted.limitations: A custom demonstration, not a built-in Hermes feature or a benchmark against other retrieval systems. It requires indexing and document-specific tools; the workflow has not been execution-tested here.

review.reason: Generic tool calls and document reading are documented; choosing pages through an explicit document hierarchy instead of vector-nearest chunks is the distinct reviewed mechanism.

closestDocs.excerpt: The `execute_code` tool lets the agent write Python scripts that call Hermes tools programmatically, collapsing multi-step workflows into a single LLM turn.
closestDocs.distinction: This explains tool composition but does not describe hierarchical PDF retrieval or PageIndex.

accepted.title: Bridge a serial terminal to Hermes with a minimal login shell
accepted.summary: A community hardware experiment connects a serial getty to a shell backed by Hermes.
accepted.author: @hugh1979
accepted.quote: Hooked the shell up to an autologin getty on a serial port.
accepted.explanation: The contributor built a minimal login shell that talks to Hermes through the gateway web service or hermes chat, then connected that shell to a serial getty. This let a physical teletype act as the input/output device without using the normal terminal interface.
accepted.limitations: A niche hardware experiment requiring a custom shell and serial setup. Autologin grants access to the attached session, so use a dedicated restricted account and control physical access. The standard CLI and API are documented; the serial-terminal bridge is the discovery.

review.reason: Official docs cover CLI and HTTP frontends but do not describe a serial getty connected to a custom Hermes login shell.

closestDocs.excerpt: The API server exposes hermes-agent as an OpenAI-compatible HTTP endpoint.
closestDocs.distinction: A generic HTTP frontend capability does not document the serial getty/login-shell bridge.

accepted.title: Block every tool at the hook level until you say go
accepted.summary: A two-command plugin keeps the agent in discussion-only mode — questions, trade-offs, a running plan — and physically cannot execute until /go.
accepted.author: @ibrandis
accepted.quote: `/converse` flips the agent into discussion-only mode. It asks clarifying questions, surfaces tradeoffs, pushes back on unclear requirements. Tools are blocked at the hook level. It physically cannot execute even if the model tries.
accepted.explanation: The contributor describes a plugin with two slash commands. /converse puts the agent into a discussion-only mode by blocking tool calls in a hook and injecting scoping instructions before each model call, so the model can ask questions and surface trade-offs but cannot act. Each reply ends with a structured plan recap. /go re-enables execution with the whole conversation already in context, so nothing has to be re-explained.
accepted.limitations: A community plugin, not a built-in mode. The source describes the design and the two hooks it uses; the archive has not run it. The built-in /plan command covers the different case of writing a plan file instead of executing.

review.reason: The distinctive mechanism is a persistent discussion-only state enforced by blocking tool calls at the hook level, with a second command that resumes execution carrying the conversation forward. Documentation describes /plan, which writes an implementation plan instead of executing a single request, and documents hooks and slash commands as plugin capabilities, but not a hook-enforced no-execution mode with a resume command.

closestDocs.excerpt: (Plan mode works the same way but is a built-in command now: `/plan [request]` tells Hermes to inspect context if needed, write a markdown implementation plan instead of executing the task, and save the result under `.hermes/plans/` relative to the active workspace/backend working directory.)
closestDocs.distinction: /plan produces a markdown plan for one request and stops; it is not a mode that stays on across turns, blocks every tool at the hook level, and is lifted by a second command that keeps the discussion in context.

closestDocs.excerpt: | Add slash commands | `ctx.register_command(name, handler, description)` — adds `/name` in CLI and gateway sessions |
closestDocs.distinction: Plugins may add slash commands; the documentation does not describe a command pair that switches tool execution off and on.

accepted.title: Subclass the OpenAI-compatible gateway so third-party chat clients keep markdown and slash commands
accepted.summary: A drop-in plugin runs a second gateway port that renders full markdown and intercepts /help, /status and the rest instead of forwarding them to the model.
accepted.author: @dworfd
accepted.quote: So I built a small drop-in plugin that fixes both. It's a separate gateway adapter (subclasses the official one, doesn't fork it), runs on its own port
accepted.explanation: Third-party OpenAI-compatible clients such as BoltAI reach Hermes through the API server, where the contributor found markdown flattened to plain text and slash commands passed to the model as ordinary messages. Rather than fork the gateway, the plugin subclasses the official adapter, listens on a second port, renders markdown and handles slash commands locally, and preserves streaming. The client is pointed at the new port and otherwise configured as the official guide describes.
accepted.limitations: A third-party plugin tested by its author with BoltAI; other OpenAI-compatible clients are stated as untested. It depends on the official gateway class it subclasses, so an upstream change could break it. Review the code before installing.

review.reason: The distinctive step is subclassing the official OpenAI-compatible gateway in a plugin to add slash-command interception and markdown rendering on a second port. Documentation routes OpenAI-compatible frontends to the API server and reserves slash commands for the TUI gateway; it describes platform adapters and registering slash commands, not extending the API server for an existing chat client.

closestDocs.excerpt: - **You want any OpenAI-compatible frontend, a language-agnostic HTTP client, or curl-driven automation** → API server.
closestDocs.distinction: The documentation sends OpenAI-compatible clients to the API server and lists slash commands under the TUI gateway, which is the gap the plugin closes.

closestDocs.excerpt: plugins/platforms/<name>/` | Gateway channel adapters (`ctx.register_platform()`) | `PluginManager` (kind: `platform`, one level deeper) |
closestDocs.distinction: Platform adapters add new messaging channels; the plugin instead wraps the existing OpenAI-compatible server for clients that already speak it.

accepted.title: Audit every profile's memory file weekly against written principles
accepted.summary: One sub-profile per project, each with its own memory, and a weekly pass that checks each memory file against a written rule of what belongs there.
accepted.author: @ogiberstein
accepted.quote: The weekly memory cleanup goes through each memory file to audit it against our 'principles of what belongs into each profile's memory'
accepted.explanation: The contributor runs a main agent plus one sub-profile per project, each keeping its own memory file. Memory still accumulates stray entries, so a scheduled weekly cleanup reads every memory file and audits it against a written statement of what belongs in each profile's memory, pruning the rest so the main agent's memory stays high-level and each project's stays specific.
accepted.limitations: A process the author runs, described in outline; the source does not include the principles document or the audit prompt. Memory files have a size cap, and what counts as belonging is the author's judgement, not a measured rule.

review.reason: The distinctive mechanism is a recurring audit of each profile's memory file against a written principles document, across per-project sub-profiles. Documentation describes MEMORY.md and USER.md, their size caps, and distillation when a session ends; it does not describe a scheduled review of memory contents against stated criteria.

closestDocs.excerpt: | **MEMORY.md** | Agent's personal notes — environment facts, conventions, things learned | 2,200 chars (~800 tokens) |
closestDocs.distinction: The documented memory is one file per agent with a character cap; the technique is a per-project set of memory files and a weekly audit of each against written principles.

closestDocs.excerpt: Memory distillation (the save before reset) also only happens when a
closestDocs.distinction: Distillation happens when a session ends; the audit is a separate scheduled pass over the saved files.
